newsitem.title: KENYA: "Great lakes" summit opens with Mandela but no Zaire.
newsitem.headline: "Great lakes" summit opens with Mandela but no Zaire.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela joined eight other leaders on Monday at a summit in Kenya on the crisis in the "Great Lakes" region but Zaire, the country at the heart of the conflict, stayed away.
The South African president, succumbing to international pressure to get involved, was taking part in high-level talks on the crisis in central Africa for the first time.
The summit began late at 5.30 p.m. (1430 GMT) and Mandela was due to fly home to Pretoria about one hour later, his spokesman Parks Mankahlana told Reuters.
Zaire's absence from the summit, apparently in protest against what it says is Rwandan and Ugandan support for a major rebellion in the east, was a blow to hopes for progress.
"It is hard to see what can be achieved without Zaire here," one delegate told Reuters.
In brief remarks to the summit's opening ceremony before the leaders went into closed session, Mandela apologised for the brevity of his stay.
He explained that South Africa's constitution barred both him and Vice-President Thabo Mbeki being abroad simultaneously.

"The whole question of the Great Lakes, particularly Zaire and Rwanda, has caught the attention of the entire world and it is absolutely necessary for us to exchange views confidentially and freely," Mandela said, suggesting that only heads of state and government remain inside the conference room in Nairobi's State House.
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi said in his opening speech it would have been "useful and helpful" if Zaire were present.
"The fact that Zaire is not here is regrettable but this must not deter us from deliberating on this problem," Moi said.

The summit, which looked likely to stretch into Tuesday, will focus on the search for a ceasefire and political settlement in eastern Zaire and review policy on Burundi, where 150,000 Hutus and Tutsis have died in ethnic war since 1993.

Rebels in eastern Zaire launched a well-planned offensive in mid-October and now control key towns. They say their ultimate goal is to end the 31-year reign of Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko who is due to return to Kinshasa on Tuesday after cancer surgery and convalescence in Europe.

The crisis in the Great Lakes -- an area roughly comprising Zaire, Burundi, Rwanda and parts of Tanzania and Uganda -- is potentially the most far-reaching in Africa since the Nigerian civil war in the late 1960s.
The French foreign ministry welcomed the Nairobi summit and hoped it would hasten the convening of an International Conference on the Great Lakes.
France has wanted such a conference for more than a year.
Zaire boycotted the first Nairobi summit on the Great Lakes last November 5, refusing to sit down with Rwanda which it accuses of sponsoring the rebellion.
Monday's boycott, despite what Moi said were assurances from Mobutu that Zaire would attend, confirmed that Kinshasa is still refusing to deal with Rwanda.
Mandela, on his first official visit to Kenya, joined the presidents of Eritrea, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe and Ethiopia's prime minister.
The rebels were not invited to take part and nor was Burundi's military regime, Kenyan officials said.
